slides.title: Nine ways to represent a single-cell matrix: the takeaways
bullets: Fly premotor neurons, 24 h APF · 16,460 cells × 19,543 genes
Summary of the v4 deck (after a strict review) · ConnectionMiner · 25 Oct 2026

slides.title: The question and the models
bullets: Nine representations of one matrix, compared on held-out prediction, synthetic ground truth and cell maps under one protocol, with uncertainty.

slides.title: 1. NB counts predict held-out detection best, and the lead is real
bullets: About 1 × 10⁻³ nats per entry ahead of every other model, with 95% intervals that exclude zero. The binary models are within 0.2 × 10⁻³ of each other.

slides.title: 2. The lead comes from bursty genes that Poisson cannot fit
bullets: NB beats Poisson at every matched rank. The gain is on observed zeros of frequently detected wiring and TF genes, where overdispersion lets a high mean coexist with a zero.

slides.title: 3. On synthetic data, each family wins the world built for it
bullets: With grids that contain the true rank, validation picks the best setting almost everywhere. NB counts win the NB world; with genuine counts they also win the low-rank logit world.

slides.title: 4. All embeddings carry hemilineage; geometry is what differs
bullets: A linear probe reads hemilineage at 0.97–0.99 from every model. Under whitening at 40 dimensions NB counts clusters best (ARI 0.74); processed counts lead at 20.

slides.title: 5. Depth is partly biology, and it hides in different places
bullets: A third of depth variance is hemilineage and birth time. Measured within those strata, scVI, Pearson residuals and NB counts keep the least depth; the binary models keep the most.

slides.title: 6. Depth-adjusted probabilities help, within limits
bullets: Setting the cell offset to the median keeps marker structure and recovers the truth on synthetic data. On real data NB's p̃ still carries some depth and also removes birth-time variation.
